newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CURLING-AUSTRALIA NOT SWEPT UP BY CURLING.
newsitem.headline: CURLING-AUSTRALIA NOT SWEPT UP BY CURLING.

text.p: The idea of men with brooms and a sport that involves sweeping is not one that sits well with the Aussie man's appetite for macho sports.
That, and just one curling rink in the whole of Australia, doesn't bode well for antipodean international success at the world curling championships in Berne.
The Aussies are certainly facing an uphill battle in their quest to qualify for the Nagano Olympics, where the sport will be granted full medal status for the first time.
Norway added to their woes on Wednesday when they handed the men from Down Under a fifth defeat in seven matches.

Although three out of the five players on the Australian squad are actually from Canada there is a growing following in Australia and the sports-mad nation will be disappointed if their men fail to make the Olympics.

"They (Australians) sort of understand the game because they've seen it on television occasionally and they relate it to lawn bowls which is a big sport in Australia," said captain Hugh Millikin, a top curler in Canada before moving to Australia in 1988. "There are only about 150 curlers in Australia."
The fact that there is just the one rink has forced Millikin and his team mates to go to great lengths to find a place to curl.

"There's no ice rink in Sydney, where three of us live, so we have to commute 900 km to Melbourne just to throw a few rocks," explained Millikin, who is attempting to raise some of the $500,000 needed to build a rink by selling 'official Australia curling team T-shirts' at the world championships.
"And it's not actually a curling rink, it's a hockey rink. We run the Zamboni (ice-cleaning machine) up and down a few times, paint some circles on the ice and throw for a few hours."
While convincing Aussies that curling is a worthy, manly pursuit is a tough enough task, enticing them off the beaches and into an icy arena is another matter all together.
"One of our Australian-born players, Jonathan Wade, sort of just came along and Steve Hewitt, well, he married a Canadian girl from Winnipeg so that sort of meant he had to learn," said Millikin.
Despite these obstacles, Australia remains the curling power in the Pacific region, champions there for the past six years ahead of Japan, South Korea and New Zealand.

Millikin's foursome represented Australia at the 1992 Albertville Olympics, finishing a respectable seventh. But the 40-year-old president of a computer software company isn't expecting to make a return appearance at the Nagano Winter Games.

"In any other year we'd be going because they would take the top eight and we're ranked eighth," said Millikin. "But this time Japan, which is ranked about 12th, gets an automatic entry so they take what would have been our spot.
"What that means is we have to finish these championships in third or fourth and either Norway or Switzerland has to finish ninth or 10th.
"Right now that isn't looking too likely -- maybe next time in Salt Lake."

In world championship competition, Millikin has taken Australia as high as fifth place in 1992 but is better remembered for his team's performance at the 1994 championships where the foursome finished 10th.

"In Oberstdorf we lost our first four games and nothing was going right," recalled Millikin. "To try to change our luck we took our little stuffed koala mascot and burned him and then went out and beat Scotland.
"It got in all the papers, I think some animal rights group thought we were actually burning koalas."
